extracted.intended_audience: Army officers, judge advocates, commanding officers, and military administrators dealing with private debts and public funds
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and explanatory guidance governing (1) what constitutes private indebtedness and when military pay/salary or property may be affected, and (2) what constitutes public money and the duties/limitations of disbursing officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of private indebtedness
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'private indebtedness' is meant an indebtedness to a private creditor as distinguished from an indebtedness to the United States or to an agency or instrumentality of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that all parties connected with the alleged indebtedness are members of the Army does not alter the private character of the indebtedness. The fact that the indebtedness has grown out of the relations of the military service does not alter its private character (citing C.14438, C.13604, etc.). Examples and case citations show boundaries of the concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances held to be private indebtedness (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific examples held to be private indebtedness: claims by a wife against her husband for support; decrees for alimony against officers or soldiers; claims based on separation agreements; claims for taxes due to a foreign commune; debts for telegraph messages or services not operated by the United States; officers' mess or post laundries operated privately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple decisions cited (e.g., C.26935; C.6882; P.61, 185) explain that even when services are connected to military life or post facilities, if the United States incurs no obligation, the indebtedness remains private and pay cannot be stopped to satisfy it (C.22200, Oct. 22, 1907/1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay not to be stopped or diverted for private indebtedness except by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: The pay of an officer or soldier cannot be stopped or diverted for the payment of private indebtedness or a private claim, except as provided by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions (C.504, C.6103, C.6882, C.13395) and the Army appropriation act of July 16, 1892 (27 Stat. 177) limit stoppages to indebtedness to the United States admitted or shown by judgment of a court. The provision empowering the Secretary of War is construed as relating only to arrears to the United States and does not authorize stopping pay to satisfy private debts.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department will not protect officers/soldiers against private suits or furnish counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers and soldiers may be sued in civil courts by private creditors; the War Department will not assist by furnishing counsel at Government expense or otherwise defend the officer to resist execution even when judgment arises out of official conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited rulings (P.64, C.23624, C.20063) state the War Department's policy to decline affirmative action to enable resistance to execution after final personal judgment; once reduced to final judgment it will be treated as indebtedness beyond dispute (see also Section V guidance on judgments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military authorities will not decide disputed private indebtedness; civil courts are proper forum
rubrics_metrics.description: The military authorities will not compel officers and soldiers to pay disputed private indebtedness or attempt to decide such disputes; creditors should resort to civil courts to establish liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If indebtedness is disputed the Department takes no enforcement role. If in the opinion of military authorities the facts and law are undisputed and no legal or equitable set-off is claimed, the officer/soldier will be advised to settle and failure may lead to trial if considered a violation of the 61st or 62nd Article of War. Investigations may be made to protect the Army's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final judgments treated as conclusive indebtedness
rubrics_metrics.description: After a claim against an officer or soldier has been reduced to a final personal judgment, if no proceedings are pending to set it aside it will be considered by the War Department as an indebtedness beyond dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation of the nature of the judgment and defenses that could have been presented to the court will not be considered to determine indebtedness in fact (judgment deemed conclusive), although such explanations/defenses may be considered to determine whether failure to satisfy the judgment constitutes a violation of the 61st or 62nd Article of War (citing C.20063, C.26858, etc.). No distinction will be made between contract and tort judgments in this respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department policy re merchants selling on credit to enlisted men
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will no longer concern itself with merchants selling merchandise to enlisted men on credit; it will decline to assist in securing payment of such obligations incurred without previous knowledge and consent of the commanding officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular (Cir.47, W.D., July 16, 1910) directs creditors/collectors to deal with commanding officers of the organizations concerned and states the Department will decline to answer inquiries or assist collection where sales were made without prior commanding-officer awareness/consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commanding officer may not enforce private debt by restricting privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Commanding officers may not enforce payment of private indebtedness by punitive measures such as denying pass privileges; such attempts to enforce payment are contrary to War Department policy and should be revoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where denying pass privileges to compel payment was held contrary to policy (C.13395, Aug. 18, 1910). Military authorities should not take actions aimed at enforcement of private debts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct since entry may support charges even if indebtedness predates service
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department will not make private indebtedness or an irregular transaction antedating entry into the service the basis of charges, but if conduct since entry in respect to matters antedating entry constitutes a military offense, charges may be preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dishonorable failure since entry to pay private indebtedness contracted before entry may properly be made the basis of charges (citing O.15088, etc.). This distinguishes the temporal focus for disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation and reporting of complaints of nonpayment against officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints of nonpayment against officers on the active list are referred to proper headquarters for necessary action; complaints need not be formal charges— a statement of acts and conduct complained of suffices as basis for investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War rulings (Nov. 18, 1897 and related documents) emphasize protecting Army character and investigating allegations, preparing formal charges only when investigation warrants such action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to submit schedule of private indebtedness when scandal threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an officer's failure to pay private debts threatens scandal to the service, superiors may lawfully order the officer to submit a schedule of all private indebtedness; refusal to obey is a violation of the 21st Article of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decision O.19525, Apr. 13, 1906 supports both the duty to investigate and the authority to order schedules of indebtedness under threat-of-scandal circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company commanders lack authority to adjudicate/apply soldier funds without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: A company commander has no authority to adjudicate and settle alleged indebtedness of a former or present soldier or to take and apply a soldier's money at the pay table to pay alleged debts without consent; he is liable to the soldier for amounts so expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (C.14439, C.13395) hold such actions wholly without authority and render the commander liable for improper application of funds taken without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest for contempt to enforce civil court support orders is allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrest of an enlisted man for contempt for not complying with a civil court order to pay maintenance for his wife is a legal proceeding and is not within the prohibition of section 1237, R.S.; it is not an arrest 'on mesne process' or 'in execution for a debt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.51, 445, Feb. 1, 1892 and related authorities treat contempt arrest as a criminal-type enforcement distinct from prohibited civil arrests for debt during enlistment; commissioned officers similarly have no general statutory exemption from arrest for debt where arrest is otherwise authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilian employee pay cannot be stopped for private indebtedness (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The salary of a civilian employee cannot be stopped for payment of private indebtedness even though it is a judgment debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.18830 (Nov. 14, 1905). However, where indebtedness or transactions show the employee loaned on the strength of office or otherwise created conditions reflecting questionable honesty, administrative action up to dismissal may be appropriate (C.27856, July 12, 1911; cases about compelling repayment under penalty of dismissal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal property necessary to military duties generally exempt from attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal property required to be possessed and used by an officer in performance of duties (e.g., sword, horse) cannot legally be seized upon attachment or execution in state court; necessary baggage on duty is likewise protected within regulation limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.33,8 (Mar. 23, 1872) and R.35,484 (Jul. 15, 1874) protect necessary property but note exemption is not to be abused — transporting excessive baggage to avoid attachments may forfeit protection and Government will not sustain such abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes public money (categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated categories that constitute 'public money' include: funds received for privileges and facilities given and sales of public property; funds received as damages; funds for use of public dry dock; funds for use of portion of water front of a reservation; fines paid under court-martial sentence; unexpended portions of prison funds when prison turned over to Dept. of Justice; money found on military reservation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual lists multiple illustrative categories (Sections I.A–N) with page references and case law guidance indicating when receipts are to be accounted as United States funds and when proceeds are not public money (e.g., proceeds from sale of abandoned civilian clothing of recruits are not public money).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursing officer—who and general responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A disbursing officer is defined and held responsible for funds in his custody; specific responsibilities include general accountability, liability for forged checks, loss of check in mail, loss of funds while being transported for payment of troops, payment 'without due care' under Army Regulations, and sending checks to contractors by mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section II (Disbursing Officers) enumerates responsibility points (1–6) and case law; disbursing officers must observe strict care and may be held accountable for failures in custody or transmission of public funds (see pages 890–893 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Garnishment, attachment, and injunctions relating to public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Funds in the hands of a disbursing officer cannot be attached or garnished; purposes of attachment cannot be accomplished by bringing suit against contractors and joining disbursing officer; attaching public funds on deposit in a bank is ineffective; subcontractors cannot control disbursement by claiming liens or filing notices with disbursing officers; injunctions against disbursing officers are limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple numbered subsections (C.1–6) explain the limits on creditors/subcontractors and judicial remedies when public funds are involved; disbursing officers should pursue remedies in their own name (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursing officer should pursue remedies in his own name relative to public money
rubrics_metrics.description: Where issues arise relative to public money, the disbursing officer should pursue remedies in his own name rather than allowing third parties to control disbursement of public funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section II.D and accompanying pages urge that the disbursing officer seek relief and protect the public treasury by appropriate proceedings, avoiding collateral attempts by private parties to interrupt public disbursement processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory provisions governing drawing and paying public money (references)
rubrics_metrics.description: References to statutory provisions: Section 3620 R.S. as to drawing check only in favor of person to whom payment is made; Section 1766 R.S. as to paying persons in arrears to the United States; where an act provides money shall be expended under direction of Secretary of War, Secretary may commit disbursement to any proper person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual lists these statutes and situates disbursing practices within these statutory constraints (see pages 893–894 and cited sections).
